# Requirements

## Scope

* Users should be given the option to start a job through the CLI.
* Users should be given the option to stop a job through the CLI.
* Users should be given the option to query the status of a job through the CLI.
* Users should be given the option to stream the output of a job through the CLI
    * When running the command, it always streams the output from the beginning of the job.
    * All streamed content is piped to stdout.
    * The order of streamed content should always be the same as the order of output generated by the job.
    * If a job has already terminated, all existing output will be streamed and the command exits.
    * The command exits when the job terminates while streaming.
    * Last but not least, streaming terminates when users interrupt.
* Users tied to different roles should have different role specific access to jobs.

## Limitations

* Only data written into stdout and stderr will be streamed
    * If the job itself is either redirecting the output to another pipeline or writing data to file(s), that part of the output will not be streamed.
        * An example of redirecting output to another pipeline can be `cat $HOME \> path/to/output/file`
        * An example of writing data to file(s) can be running `make build` in a local codebase which creates an executable binary while writing logs into stdout. In this case, only those logs will be streamed.
        * If users really want those files created by jobs, they can simply fire up new jobs to stream the content of those files.
* No per-stream separation on the CLI side:
    * CLI users won’t be able to independently redirect or filter stdout vs stderr.
        * On the gRPC server side, merge the child’s stderr into stdout and stream a single FD.
        * This preserves the kernel’s single serialized order and drops the complexity.
* No shutdown/crash recovery because adding such a mechanism means:
    * Additional persistent layers to track job information such as job ID and path of the job’s log output.
    * Detaching jobs from the application so that they keep running and logging even when the application dies.
    * Attaching to external tools such as an inotify queue to receive log file update events and process them.
* Job outputs won’t be persisted and instead will be stored in memory.
* We will only enforce user-level security at the API level. If we want to stop an attacker from bypassing the authn/authz system, we need to enforce Linux user-level security which requires:
    * Running the application as a root user.
    * After the API level authn/authz, translate the external user into an internal user on the Linux host.
    * Create the process with the translated internal user’s UID and place the process within a cgroup.

# Technical Design

## TLS Setup

Out of scope:
* For simplicity, we will just use a self-signed root CA to sign both the client's cert and the server's cert.
    * In production, we will use real CAs and intermediate CAs to sign the certs.
* For simplicity, we will not rotate the root CA.
    * In production, we will rotate the root CA periodically.
* For simplicity, we will not pin issuers by AKI/SKI and instead will just verify the issuer's subject.
    * In production, we will pin issuers by AKI/SKI.

Both API and CLI will enforce:
* Using TLS 1.3.
* Using P-384 as the preferred key exchange curve, then P-256 and X25519 for maximizing compatibility.
    * P-384 is a bit slower than the other two, but it is more secure.
* Using ECDSAWithP384AndSHA384 as the preferred signature scheme, then Ed25519 and ECDSAWithP256AndSHA256 for maximizing compatibility.
* Using ECDSA P-384 as the preferred key type, then Ed25519 and ECDSA P-256 for maximizing compatibility.
* SAN required which means certs with only CN will be rejected.
* Pinning the issuer of the cert.
* Expiry date time of the cert. (Go already checks NotBefore and NotAfter but just include it here for completeness)

Validations required only on the API side:
* EKU must include ClientAuth and KU must include DigitalSignature.
* SAN must contain the SPIFFE ID of the client (prefixed with `spiffe://jobmgr/cli`) and an email address (serves as the owner of the job).
* Custom OID for embedding RBAC rules must be present.

Validations required only on the CLI side:
* EKU must include ServerAuth and KU must include DigitalSignature.
* SAN must contain the SPIFFE ID of the API (prefixed with `spiffe://jobmgr/api`) and the hostname/IP of API.

All of these will be enforced during the mTLS handshake, connections will be rejected if any of the validations fail.
And because of that, CLI will never see an unauthenticated error because if authentication fails, the request won't even reach the API handler.

## RBAC

### Roles

#### Dev Role (Owner Scoped)

Devs can start new jobs,
stop their own existing jobs,
list their own existing jobs,
query the status or stream the output of their own existing jobs.
They cannot view or stop jobs started by other users.

#### Read-Only Admin Role

Read-only admins can list all existing jobs,
Query status and stream output of any existing job regardless of the owner of the job.
They cannot start new jobs or stop existing jobs.

#### Read-Write Admin Role

Read-write admins can start new jobs,
stop any existing job,
list all existing jobs,
query the status or stream the output of any existing job regardless of the owner of the job.

### Resource Attributes

#### Start Job

The operation requires users to have:
* create job access.

#### Stop Job

The operation requires users to have:
* get job with the required owner.
* stop job with the required owner.

#### List Jobs

The operation requires users to have:
* list jobs with the required owner.

#### Query Job Status

The operation requires users to have:
* get job with the required owner.
* get job status with the required owner.

#### Stream Output

The operation requires users to have:
* get job with the required owner.
* get job status with the required owner.
* get job output with the required owner.

## API

### JobServer

#### JobService

##### Workflow

After the mTLS handshake, on receiving a request, the JobService:
* Read the user's email from the cert's SAN and RBAC rules from the cert's custom OID.
* Retrieve the operation’s required resource attributes.
* Compare the user's RBAC rules with the operation’s required resource attributes to determine whether the user has the permission to perform the operation.
* If the user does not have the permission, return an error.
* If the user has the permission, delegate the operation to the underlying JobManager.

##### Associated Protos

```protobuf
syntax = "proto3";
package jobmgr.job;
option go_package = "github.com/xiumozhan/jobmgr/api/jobpb;jobpb";
import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto";

service JobService {
  rpc StartJob(StartJobRequest) returns (StartJobResponse);
  rpc StopJob(StopJobRequest) returns (StopJobResponse);
  rpc ListJobs(ListJobsRequest) returns (ListJobsResponse);
  rpc GetJobStatus(GetJobStatusRequest) returns (GetJobStatusResponse);
  rpc StreamOutput(StreamOutputRequest) returns (stream Log);
}

message EnvVar {
  string key   = 1;
  string value = 2;
}

message StartJobRequest {
  string command       = 1;
  repeated string args = 2;
  repeated EnvVar env  = 3;
}

message StartJobResponse {
  string job_id = 1;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp started_at = 2;
}

message StopJobRequest {
  string job_id = 1;
}

message StopJobResponse {
  string job_id    = 1;
  bool   stopped   = 2;
  int32  exit_code = 3;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp stopped_at = 4;
}

enum JobStatus {
  JOB_RUNNING    = 0;
  JOB_COMPLETED  = 1;
  JOB_ERROR      = 2;
  JOB_TERMINATED = 3;
}

message ListJobsRequest {}

message ListJobsResponse {
  repeated string jobs = 1;
}

message GetJobStatusRequest {
  string job_id = 1;
}

message GetJobStatusResponse {
  JobStatus status = 1;
}

message StreamOutputRequest {
  string job_id = 1;
}

message Log {
  bytes data = 1;
}
```

#### JobManager

##### Associated Go API

```go
type Job interface {
    ID() uuid.UUID
    GetStatus() Status
    Owner() string
    StartedAt() *time.Time
    StoppedAt() *time.Time
    Stop()
    StreamOutput() Streamer
}

type Streamer interface {
    Stream() <-chan []byte
    Close()
}

type JobManager interface {
    Start(owner string, spec job.Spec) (job.Job, error)
    Stop(id uuid.UUID) (job.Job, error)
    List(owner string) ([]job.Job, error)
    Get(id uuid.UUID) (job.Job, error)
    StreamOutput(id uuid.UUID) (job.Streamer, error)
}
```

##### Job

A job is a wrapper around a process, maintains an in-memory log buffer.
It also handles the communication between the JobManager and the underlying process:

* In addition to the PID of the underlying process, each job has a unique UUID generated by the `JobManager` at the time of creation.
* The job waits for its underlying process to finish and updates its status accordingly.
* The job handles incoming requests to stop itself.
* The job handles incoming requests to stream its output by creating a streamer.
* The job continuously reads from stdout and stderr of its underlying process and writes the logs into its log buffer.
    * The log buffer is a byte slice guarded by an RWMutex.
    * Any writing to the log buffer will acquire the write lock and release it when done.
    * Any reading from the log buffer will acquire the read lock and release it when done.

A job can have the following status:
* `RUNNING`: The job is currently running.
* `COMPLETED`: The job has completed successfully.
* `ERROR`: The job ended on its own (not terminated by the `JobManager`) but unsuccessfully such as exit with non-zero exit code.
* `TERMINATED`: The job has been terminated by the `JobManager`.

##### Streamer

A streamer:
* Waits for job's notification on every writing of new logs through `sync.Cond`.
    * Every time it waits, it checks if the log output has been stopped. If so, it stops waiting and drains the log buffer and closes the stream.
* Reads from the log buffer and writes the logs to the stream.
* Upon receiving a notification on the size of the log, the streamer:
    * If the size of logs it is notified with is greater than the size of logs it has read, it reads logs from the log buffer until it reaches the end of the log buffer.
    * After each read, it updates the size of logs it has read.
    * If the latest size of logs is less than the size of logs it has read, skips the read and continues to wait for the next notification.
* Upon receiving a stop signal, it closes the stream.

## CLI

### Start Job

* Accepted command:
    * `jobmgr start [-e KEY=VALUE] COMMAND [ARG…]`
* Interact gRPC API:
    * `JobService.StartJob`

### Stop Job

* Accepted command:
    * `jobmgr stop <jobID>`
* Interact gRPC API:
    * `JobService.StopJob`

### List Jobs

* Accepted command:
    * `jobmgr ls`
* Interact gRPC API:
    * `JobService.ListJobs`

### Query Job Status

* Accepted command:
    * `jobmgr status <jobID>`
* Interact gRPC API:
    * `JobService.GetJobStatus`

### Stream Job Output

* Accepted command:
    * `jobmgr stream <jobID>`
* Interact gRPC API:
    * `JobService.StreamOutput`
